body:
The end of an urban civilisation

The Harappan or Indus Civilisation was one of the earliest urban civilisations of the Indian subcontinent. During its Mature Harappan phase, approximately 2600–1900 BCE, it was characterised by planned cities, organised drainage, standardised weights, seals, writing, specialised crafts and extensive exchange networks.

After approximately 1900 BCE, this urban system underwent major changes. Large cities declined or were abandoned, long-distance exchange weakened, and many people lived in smaller settlements. However, these changes did not mean that the entire Harappan population disappeared.

De-urbanisation

De-urbanisation means the decline of large towns and urban institutions, accompanied by a greater importance of smaller settlements and rural activities. In the Harappan context, it describes the weakening of the earlier city-based system, not the extinction of its people.

The main chronological stages

The transition was gradual and varied from region to region. The following dates are approximate rather than exact beginning or ending years for every settlement.

PeriodApproximate chronologyMain characteristic
Early HarappanBefore 2600 BCERegional settlements and growing towns preceded mature urban development.
Mature Harappan2600–1900 BCELarge planned cities and widespread cultural standardisation.
Late HarappanAfter 1900 BCESmaller settlements, regional variations and continued habitation in several areas.

By approximately 1800 BCE, most Mature Harappan sites in areas such as Cholistan, in present-day Pakistan, had been abandoned. At the same time, new settlements appeared or expanded in parts of Gujarat, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh.

What changed in the cities?

The weakening of urban organisation is visible in several connected developments:

  • Writing and seals: the distinctive Harappan script and seals ceased to be widely used.
  • Weights: the earlier system of standardised weights was increasingly replaced by local practices.
  • Crafts: specialised production of objects such as distinctive beads declined in many places.
  • Trade: the extensive long-distance exchange characteristic of the Mature Harappan period diminished.
  • Buildings: construction of large public structures declined, and some cities showed poorer maintenance or alteration of earlier buildings.

At Mohenjodaro, for example, later occupation showed neglected drainage, accumulated refuse and buildings constructed over earlier streets. These changes indicate a weakening of the former urban organisation. They do not, by themselves, establish why it weakened.

Decline of the civilisation's urban system is different from disappearance of its population. The transformation occurred over time, and some places remained inhabited even after their Mature Harappan features declined.

Prelims focus

  • The Mature Harappan phase is generally dated to approximately 2600–1900 BCE.
  • Major urban transformation began around 1900 BCE.
  • By approximately 1800 BCE, most Mature Harappan sites in Cholistan had been abandoned.
  • Late Harappan settlements generally showed a more rural and regionally varied way of life.
  • Trap: The end of Mature Harappan urbanism did not mean that all Harappan settlements disappeared simultaneously.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Theme 1, 'Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation', pp. 1 and 17; NCERT, Class 6, Our Pasts–I, Chapter 4, 'In the Earliest Cities', pp. 40–41.]

pictures.caption: Urban life during the Mature Harappan period.

title: The Harappan Decline: What Changed and When?

body:
Why rainfall mattered to the cities

Harappan cities depended on food supplied by farmers and herders living in the surrounding countryside. Agriculture, in turn, depended on rainfall, river water, seasonal flooding and locally available water-storage arrangements.

A reduction in rainfall could therefore affect a city even when the city itself was not directly damaged. If harvests became less reliable, the supply of food to urban populations could weaken. This would make it more difficult to sustain large settlements and people engaged primarily in specialised crafts, trade and other non-agricultural work.

A drier climate

Climatic changes are an important proposed explanation for the Harappan transformation. Rainfall became less reliable in parts of northwestern South Asia during the later Mature Harappan period. A broader phase of increasing dryness is commonly associated with the period from approximately 2200 BCE onward.

Reduced rainfall could have affected agricultural production, pastures and the flow of rivers dependent on the monsoon. Recent research also indicates that repeated or prolonged periods of river drought may have contributed to the movement of populations away from major urban centres.

However, the intensity and timing of dry conditions differed between regions. Climate change is therefore an important contributing factor, not a complete explanation for the fate of every Harappan settlement.

River changes and water availability

The location and reliability of rivers were important for Harappan settlements. A river that changed course, carried less water or became less dependable could affect nearby farming, transport and access to water.

The Ghaggar–Hakra system, associated with settlements in parts of Haryana, Rajasthan and Cholistan, is particularly relevant. The modern Ghaggar is largely seasonal. Reduced monsoon-fed water availability may have affected some communities in this wider region. Sites such as Kalibangan in Rajasthan and Banawali in Haryana are important examples when studying the relationship between Harappan settlements and changing river environments.

A distinction is necessary here. It would be incorrect to state that one large perennial river suddenly changed course in 1900 BCE and thereby destroyed the entire civilisation. Research on an ancient course of the Sutlej indicates that its major diversion occurred long before the Mature Harappan urban period. The effects of later rainfall and seasonal-water changes must be considered separately from that much earlier river diversion.

River change is not one single event

River diversion means a river changes its course. Reduced river flow means less water passes through a channel. Seasonal flow means water is available mainly during particular seasons. These are different conditions and need not have occurred together at every Harappan site.

How environmental stress could affect urban life

The possible relationship between climate and settlement change can be understood as a sequence: less reliable rainfall may reduce water availability and agricultural output; this may weaken the ability of surrounding villages to support large towns; people may then move towards places where farming and water supplies remain more dependable.

This sequence explains a possible mechanism rather than a proven identical chain of events at every site. Local floods could also damage particular settlements, showing why both water shortage and excess water appear among the proposed causes of decline.

Prelims focus

  • Increasing dryness from around 2200 BCE onward is an important climatic context for the later Harappan period.
  • Reduced rainfall could affect cities indirectly by weakening agricultural food supplies.
  • The Ghaggar–Hakra system is associated with important Harappan settlement areas.
  • Kalibangan is in Rajasthan; Banawali is in Haryana.
  • Trap: Neither a single drought nor the sudden diversion of one river in 1900 BCE has been established as the cause of the decline of every Harappan city.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 6, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Chapter 6, 'The Beginnings of Indian Civilisation', pp. 102–103; NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Theme 1, p. 17; Singh et al., 'Counter-intuitive influence of Himalayan river morphodynamics on Indus Civilisation urban settlements', Nature Communications, 2017, Abstract and Discussion, accessed 17 November 2026; Solanki et al., 'River drought forcing of the Harappan metamorphosis', Communications Earth & Environment, 2025, Abstract and Discussion, accessed 17 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Farming communities adapting to a drier environment.

title: Climate Change and River Systems in the Harappan Decline

body:
No single explanation fits every region

The Harappan Civilisation covered a very large geographical area. Its settlements differed in their rivers, rainfall, agricultural conditions and economic activities. A flood could damage one settlement while a shortage of water affected another. A change in trade might harm a specialised production centre more than a farming village.

For this reason, the decline is best understood as a multi-causal process: several environmental, economic and organisational difficulties may have acted together, but their relative importance varied across regions.

Major proposed causes and their limitations

Proposed factorPossible effectImportant limitation
Reduced rainfall and droughtLess reliable water, crops and pastures.Dry conditions did not affect all regions equally.
River changesSome settlements lost dependable nearby water or transport routes.River histories differed from one area to another.
Excessive floodingDamage to buildings, fields and particular settlements.Floods at one site cannot explain the decline of distant cities.
Deforestation and overgrazingPossible pressure on vegetation and other local resources.These suggestions are not established as a civilisation-wide cause.
Weakening of exchange networksReduced movement of materials and demand for specialised goods.Trade decline may have been both a consequence and a contributing factor.
Weakening of urban authorityDifficulty maintaining common standards and large public works.The exact form of Harappan political authority remains uncertain.

Environmental and economic changes could reinforce one another

Consider a Harappan town that depended on surrounding villages for grain and on distant settlements for raw materials. If agricultural supplies became unreliable, the town might find it harder to support specialised workers. If exchange networks also weakened, those workers might have fewer materials and fewer opportunities to trade their products. The combined effect could make a smaller, more locally supported settlement more practical.

This example illustrates how problems could reinforce one another. It does not prove that this precise sequence occurred at every Harappan town.

The decline of common urban organisation

The Mature Harappan world had unusually widespread similarities in bricks, seals and weights. After 1900 BCE, such shared features became less prominent in many regions. Instead of the earlier common system of measurement and exchange, local practices gained importance.

This change suggests that the ability to maintain widespread urban coordination had weakened. It may reflect the decline of institutions or authorities that helped organise production, exchange and construction. However, the disappearance of standardised objects cannot by itself establish exactly how the earlier political system operated.

Observed change and proposed cause are different. The disappearance of standardised weights is evidence of changed economic organisation. It is not direct proof that drought, invasion or the fall of a particular ruler caused that change.

Prelims focus

  • The Harappan decline is commonly explained through a combination of environmental, economic and organisational factors.
  • Flooding is a possible cause of damage at particular sites, not a sufficient explanation for the entire civilisation.
  • Deforestation and overgrazing are proposed environmental pressures, not proven universal causes.
  • The declining use of seals, script and standardised weights indicates a loss of earlier cultural and economic uniformity.
  • Trap: A decline in long-distance trade may be both an effect of urban weakening and a factor that intensified it.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 6, Our Pasts–I, Chapter 4, 'In the Earliest Cities', pp. 40–41; NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Theme 1, 'The End of the Civilisation', p. 17; Solanki et al., 'River drought forcing of the Harappan metamorphosis', Communications Earth & Environment, 2025, Abstract and Discussion, accessed 17 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Several possible pressures may interact; observed urban changes are distinct, and regional differences prevent any single civilisation-wide explanation.
pictures.caption: Several pressures could interact without having identical effects everywhere.

title: Why the Harappan Decline Had Multiple Causes

body:
Where did people go?

Harappan de-urbanisation was accompanied by changes in the distribution of settlements. As several older urban centres declined, habitation expanded into other areas.

By approximately 1800 BCE, most Mature Harappan sites in regions such as Cholistan had been abandoned. During the broader period of change, settlement expanded in parts of Gujarat, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh. Many of the settlements associated with the later phase were smaller and had a more rural character.

These developments support the idea of population dispersal: people and communities became more widely distributed across different settlements rather than remaining concentrated in the earlier major urban centres.

Population dispersal

Population dispersal is the spreading of people across different locations. In the Harappan case, it helps describe the movement towards smaller settlements and the changing regional distribution of habitation.

Migration is not the same as invasion

Migration means movement of people from one area to another. It may occur gradually for several reasons, including access to water, farmland, pastures or better living conditions.

Invasion means entry into a territory by force, generally involving armed conflict. Evidence that populations shifted towards new settlements does not by itself establish that an invading army destroyed the earlier cities.

Why the invasion explanation is not accepted as a general cause

An older explanation attributed the collapse of Harappan cities to a violent invasion, sometimes described as an Aryan invasion. This interpretation is not supported by convincing evidence of a widespread, simultaneous military destruction of the urban centres.

Human remains found at Mohenjodaro were once interpreted as evidence of a massacre. However, the remains did not establish that all those individuals died in the same event, and the site did not show the widespread destruction expected from a single final assault. Consequently, a violent invasion is not regarded as an established explanation for the end of Mature Harappan urbanism.

This does not mean that no people ever migrated into or within the subcontinent during ancient times. It means that the specific claim of an invasion destroying the Harappan civilisation has not been demonstrated.

Understanding the Late Harappan population

Some communities continued to occupy former Harappan areas, while others lived in newly established settlements. Their activities and objects became increasingly regional. Thus, the Late Harappan period represents both movement and continuity.

The available evidence does not allow every movement of population to be reconstructed or assigned to a single cause. In particular, environmental pressure may explain movement in some areas without proving that all communities migrated for the same reason.

Prelims focus

  • Cholistan: many Mature Harappan settlements were abandoned by approximately 1800 BCE.
  • Gujarat, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh: important areas of settlement expansion during the transformation.
  • Population dispersal means people spreading across different settlements.
  • Migration does not necessarily involve warfare or conquest.
  • Trap: A violent invasion is not an established civilisation-wide explanation for Harappan decline.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Theme 1, pp. 17–18, including 'The End of the Civilisation' and 'Evidence of an Invasion'; NCERT, Class 6, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Chapter 6, pp. 102–103.]

pictures.caption: Movement to new settlements is not evidence of military conquest.

title: Migration, Settlement Dispersal and the Invasion Hypothesis
